cards.front: An {{c1::inherited trait}} is a trait passed from parents to offspring through genes, such as eye color or the shape of a pea seed.
cards.quote: An inherited trait is a trait passed from parents to offspring through genes, such as eye color or the shape of a pea seed.
cards.section: Explain: what can be passed on

cards.front: An {{c1::acquired trait}} is a characteristic a living thing gets during its life, such as a scar, dyed hair, a skill like playing piano, or muscles built by exercise.
cards.quote: An acquired trait is a characteristic a living thing gets during its life, such as a scar, dyed hair, a skill like playing piano, muscles built by exercise, or the language you speak.
cards.section: Explain: what can be passed on

cards.front: Why does a scar on a parent not get passed on to the parent's young?
cards.back: Young grow from sex cells, an egg and a sperm. A scar changes body cells, not the genes in the sex cells.
cards.quote: A scar or exercise changes body cells, not the genes in sex cells.
cards.section: Explain: what can be passed on

cards.front: Your {{c1::phenotype}} is the trait that shows, such as purple or white flowers.
cards.quote: Your phenotype is the trait that shows, such as purple or white flowers.
cards.section: Explain: genes and environment work together

cards.front: In garden soil, what does a lower pH number tell you?
cards.quote: Gardeners measure acidity with soil pH, a number where lower means more acidic.
cards.section: Explain: genes and environment work together

cards.front: Two cuttings from one color-changing hydrangea have the same genes, yet one blooms blue and one blooms pink. Why?
cards.back: In many kinds, acidic soil lets the roots take up more aluminum, which turns the flowers blue; less acidic soil gives pink.
cards.why: The genes are the same, so the environment decided which color showed.
cards.quote: In many kinds, acidic soil lets the roots take up more aluminum, which turns the flowers blue; less acidic soil gives pink.
cards.section: Explain: genes and environment work together

cards.front: Why is a person's height an example of genes and environment working together?
cards.back: Height depends on many genes and also on food and health while you grow.
cards.quote: Your height depends on many genes and on food and health while you grow.
cards.section: Explain: genes and environment work together

cards.front: A color-changing hydrangea blooms blue in acidic soil of pH about 5.2. A cutting from it is planted in soil above pH 7. What color do you expect, and why?
cards.back: Pink. The cutting has the same genes, but less acidic soil gives pink flowers. The soil, not the genes, changed the phenotype.
cards.quote: In many kinds, acidic soil lets the roots take up more aluminum, which turns the flowers blue; less acidic soil gives pink.
cards.section: Explain: genes and environment work together

cards.front: In the garden simulation, a plant has two white alleles. You slide the soil from acidic to less acidic. Does the flower color change?
cards.back: No. The white alleles block color, so there is no color for the soil to change. The genes set which colors are possible.
cards.quote: A plant carries color alleles, or white alleles that block color, and you set the soil from acidic to less acidic.
cards.section: Explore: grow a garden of genes and soil

cards.front: A {{c1::recessive}} allele shows its trait only when both copies are recessive.
cards.quote: A recessive allele shows its trait only when both copies are recessive.
cards.section: Explain: dominant does not mean common

cards.front: Does a dominant allele mean most people have its trait? Explain.
cards.back: No. Dominant tells how an allele shows, because one copy is enough. It does not tell how common the trait is.
cards.quote: Key idea: Dominant tells how an allele shows, not how common it is.
cards.section: Explain: dominant does not mean common

cards.front: A gardener dyes the petals of a parent plant, then grows its seeds. What color will the young plants' petals show, and why?
cards.back: The young show the color their own genes and soil give, not the dye. Dye changes the parent's petals, not the genes in its sex cells.
cards.quote: A scar or exercise changes body cells, not the genes in sex cells.
cards.section: Explain: what can be passed on

cards.front: Weismann cut the tails off white mice and bred them, for five generations of parents, then checked the young. If a cut tail could be inherited, what would the young show? What did he find?
cards.back: If it were inherited, some young would have short or abnormal tails. He found none: 0 of 901 young. Cut tails were not inherited.
cards.quote: He did this to the parents for five generations and looked at the young's tails.
cards.section: Elaborate: cut tails and counted traits

cards.front: In Weismann's experiment, the five groups of young numbered 333, 237, 152, 138 and 41, with 0 short or abnormal tails in each. What fraction of all the young had short or abnormal tails?
cards.back: 333 + 237 + 152 + 138 + 41 = 901 young. The fraction is 0 out of 901, which is 0.
cards.quote: Predict 3. Add the young in the five groups. What fraction had short or abnormal tails?
cards.section: Elaborate: cut tails and counted traits

cards.front: Rh-negative blood (recessive) is about 15 per 100 people of European ancestry. A small extra finger (thought dominant) is 0.035 per 100 in one group. About how many times more common is Rh-negative blood?
cards.back: 15 / 0.035 is about 430 times as common, a rough comparison, since the groups and counting methods differ. A recessive trait can be far more common than a dominant one.
cards.quote: Rh-negative blood is about 15 / 0.035, or roughly 430 times, as common as the extra-finger trait in the 0.035 row.
cards.section: Elaborate: cut tails and counted traits

cards.front: Why is comparing the extra-finger counts with the Rh-negative counts only a rough comparison?
cards.back: The rows are different groups counted in different ways. It is not a controlled test.
cards.quote: These are different groups counted in different ways, so the rows are a rough comparison, not a controlled test.
cards.section: Elaborate: cut tails and counted traits

cards.front: An old idea said giraffes stretched their necks and passed longer necks to their young. Why do scientists not accept it?
cards.back: Using a body part changes body cells, not the genes in sex cells.
cards.quote: Scientists do not accept it, because using a body part changes body cells, not the genes in sex cells.
cards.section: An old inheritance idea

cards.front: You grow 5 stem cuttings from one coleus in bright light and 5 in shade, with the same pots, soil, water and temperature. The groups end up different heights. What does that show? What if the cuttings came from 10 different plants?
cards.back: With one plant, the genes are the same, so the environment (light) changed the phenotype. With 10 different plants, genes could also differ, so you could not tell.
cards.why: Rule: cuttings from one plant share genes, so only the environment differs.
cards.quote: If the groups differ, the environment changed the phenotype, since the genes were the same.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A change in one branch of a plant can show up in plants grown from its cuttings, but a scar on a mouse never shows up in its young. What explains the difference?
cards.back: A cutting is made of body cells, so it carries the branch's change. Animal young grow from sex cells, and a scar changes body cells, not those genes.
cards.why: Rests on: a scar changes body cells, not the genes in sex cells.
cards.quote: Plants are different: a cutting is made of body cells, so a change in one branch can show up in plants grown from its cuttings.
cards.section: Plants, sex cells and parents’ experiences

cards.front: A student says: "Dominant alleles make a trait common, and learned skills can be passed on if you practice hard enough." Use the lesson's two rules to correct both claims.
cards.back: Dominant tells how an allele shows, not how common it is, so a dominant trait can be rare, like the extra finger. A learned skill is acquired: it changes body cells, not the genes in sex cells, so it is not passed on.
cards.quote: The small extra finger is thought to be passed on by a dominant allele, but few people carry that allele, so the trait is rare.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking
